title: The National Practitioner Data Bank -- Definition/Introduction
content: The National Practitioner Data Bank (NPDB) is a centralized database overseen by the United States Department of Health and Human Services that collects reports of medical malpractice and other adverse actions taken against health care workers. Information is submitted to NPDB by agencies such as hospitals, state licensing boards, and medical malpractice insurance companies. The records the NPDB compiles include healthcare-related criminal convictions and civil judgments (eg, medical malpractice), final decisions rendered in licensure and certification actions, and other adjudicated actions. Information in the database is used to make employment decisions, track a physician's records, and support medical privileging. The records in NPDB are protected, and only authorized users (ie, hospitals or state licensure boards) can obtain a physician's record via a query. [1]

title: The National Practitioner Data Bank -- Issues of Concern
content: Congress created the NPDB with the intent to increase patient safety, combat health care fraud, and improve medical care amid the rising volume of Medical Malpractice Litigation. title: The National Practitioner Data Bank -- Issues of Concern
content: Section 1921 (Enacted in 1987) permits the Federal Government to collect information on licensure sanctions against physicians, health care entities, and dentists. Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1990 to add the language "any negative action or finding" from entities such as peer review organizations, private accreditation entities, or state licensure regulators. Modified Regulations for Section 1921 were published in the Federal Register on January 28, 2010, to create a national control program to oversee fraud and abuse by health care entities and clinicians.

title: The National Practitioner Data Bank -- Issues of Concern
content: The NPDB is not meant to be the sole avenue for verifying a clinician's credentials, nor is it solely a system to determine whether a more extensive investigation should take place. An example of where this is applicable is a medical malpractice settlement, which will be displayed in the NPDB; however, settlements of medical malpractice can be made for a variety of different practical reasons and may not be representative of a physician lacking competence or engaging in conduct that did not meet the standard of care. Additionally, one of the critical issues for the NPDB is maintaining the confidentiality, accuracy, and security of the database, as regulated by 45 CFR Part 60. To protect the security and confidentiality of the information, the NPDB  ensures that sensitive financial and personal information is protected from unauthorized users. [2] [3]

title: The National Practitioner Data Bank -- Clinical Significance
content: Unfortunately, throughout a clinician's career, they may be subjected to a report that was submitted by a reporting entity, such as a malpractice judgment or settlement. This report would follow the clinician for the remainder of the clinician's career unless the information submitted were found to be factually incorrect. After receiving a report, the NPDB will notify the subject and advise the clinician on how to obtain the record. Additionally, the NPDB will explain to the clinician named in a record the process for adding a statement or disputing the report. [4]

title: The National Practitioner Data Bank -- Clinical Significance
content: Additionally, clinicians need to be aware that there are many definitions of reportable events to the NPDB. Since hospitals are required to report a physician's resignation while an investigation is underway to the NPDB, clinicians should receive in writing that they are not subject to any inquiry before resigning, to ensure they maintain their rights and have a chance to defend their reputation if they are subject to any investigations. Furthermore, clinicians should stay informed about changes to the NDPB throughout their careers, as adverse reports can make it challenging to obtain or renew hospital privileges.
